# The Lantern Keeper

For two years, Mara had studied the routines of Greyhaven's lighthouse under Ivo: polishing the lens, trimming the wick, carrying measured oil, checking the shutters, recording the weather, and learning how the harbour's evening tide narrowed the safe route around Black Tooth Reef.

A severe autumn squall arrived before dusk. While securing a shutter, Ivo was thrown against the wall and twisted his ankle badly enough that he could not manage the spiral stairs. The main lantern remained unlit even though the Gull Star, a trading vessel carrying a rival merchant's valuable cloth, was expected before nightfall.

Magistrate Rusk arrived at precisely that moment. He held administrative authority over the papers apprentices needed before qualifying for harbour work, and he also had a financial interest in which merchant vessel obtained the first berth. He instructed Mara to postpone illumination for ten minutes so the Gull Star would be forced to turn back and his own ship could take priority.

When Mara refused, Rusk made the pressure explicit. He warned that her apprenticeship paperwork might never be accepted if she disobeyed him.

Mara considered the personal cost with considerable anxiety. Her training represented two years of labour and the profession she intended to enter. Nevertheless, the lantern's purpose was to give approaching crews a reliable visual marker when rain and darkness concealed Black Tooth Reef. Rusk's threat altered the risk to Mara but not the navigational danger to the ship.

Ivo directed her to the reserve oil. Mara carried the heavy can upstairs, cleared rainwater from the lantern housing, replenished the reservoir, prepared the wick, and established a steady flame before the Gull Star reached the reef. The captain saw the light, adjusted the ship's course, and passed safely into Greyhaven.

Afterward, Mara gave Ivo an exact account of Rusk's demand and threat. Ivo reported it to the harbour council. Other workers supplied similar accounts, so the council removed Rusk's authority over apprenticeship papers during its investigation. Mara received no immediate promotion or public prize; she continued her apprenticeship, with Ivo's quiet trust shown the next evening when he handed her the oil can.
